questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with HFrEF has taken enalapril for 2 years. His cardiologist stops enalapril and, after a short washout period, starts sacubitril-valsartan. Three months later he can walk farther without dyspnea, and his leg edema is less. His laboratory values before the switch and 3 months later are: BNP 410 pg/mL, now 520 pg/mL; NT-proBNP 2,600 pg/mL, now 1,500 pg/mL; serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, now 1.2 mg/dL. Which mechanism best explains the change in his BNP level?
choices: Greater ventricular wall stretch from worsening heart failure
Lower renal clearance of BNP from a fall in filtration
Less enzymatic breakdown of BNP by neprilysin
Direct stimulation of BNP gene expression by valsartan
Assay interference from antibodies against the drug
questions.explanation: Sacubitril inhibits **neprilysin**, the enzyme that breaks down natriuretic peptides, so **BNP rises as a drug effect**. **NT-proBNP** is not a neprilysin substrate, so its fall shows that wall stress is actually lower, which matches his clinical improvement. Worsening heart failure would raise both markers and worsen his symptoms, and the very small creatinine change cannot explain the BNP rise.
questions.explanation_pt: O sacubitril inibe a **neprilisina**, enzima que degrada os peptídeos natriuréticos, então o **BNP sobe como efeito do medicamento**. O **NT-proBNP** não é substrato da neprilisina, e sua queda mostra que o estresse parietal está de fato menor, o que combina com a melhora clínica. A piora da insuficiência cardíaca elevaria os dois marcadores e pioraria os sintomas, e a variação mínima da creatinina não explica a alta do BNP.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman with HFrEF takes lisinopril, carvedilol and furosemide. Spironolactone is added to her treatment. At a routine visit 10 days later she feels well. Her laboratory values before the new drug and now are: potassium 4.7 mEq/L, now 6.1 mEq/L; sodium 138 mEq/L, now 136 mEq/L; creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, now 1.5 mg/dL; bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, now 21 mEq/L. Which action of the new drug best explains the rise in her potassium?
choices: Blocked aldosterone action in collecting duct principal cells
Inhibition of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
Shift of potassium out of cells from beta-receptor blockade
Lower aldosterone secretion from reduced angiotensin II formation
Inhibition of the Na-K ATPase in skeletal muscle cells
questions.explanation: Spironolactone blocks the **mineralocorticoid receptor** in **principal cells**. Less ENaC activity means less sodium reabsorption, a less negative tubular lumen, and less **potassium secretion**, so **hyperkalemia** develops, especially with an ACE inhibitor. Lower aldosterone from reduced angiotensin II is the mechanism of lisinopril, which she already took before the potassium rose; it adds to the risk but is not the action of the new drug.
questions.explanation_pt: A espironolactona bloqueia o **receptor mineralocorticoide** nas **células principais**. Com menos atividade do ENaC, há menos reabsorção de sódio, um lúmen tubular menos negativo e menor **secreção de potássio**, levando a **hipercalemia**, sobretudo junto com um IECA. A redução da aldosterona por menor formação de angiotensina II é o mecanismo do lisinopril, que ela já usava antes de o potássio subir; ele soma risco, mas não é a ação do novo medicamento.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 30% says that he now sleeps on three pillows. When he lies flat, he becomes short of breath within a few minutes. Sitting up relieves the dyspnea. Which change that happens when he lies down best explains this symptom?
choices: Less venous return that lowers left ventricular stroke volume
Higher systemic vascular resistance from sympathetic activation
Compression of the main bronchi by an enlarged left atrium
Lower respiratory drive from the medullary centers
More venous return that raises pulmonary capillary pressure
questions.explanation: Lying flat moves blood from the legs and abdomen into the chest, so **venous return and preload rise**. A failing left ventricle works on the flat part of its **Frank-Starling curve**, so it cannot eject the extra volume; left atrial and **pulmonary capillary pressures** rise and fluid moves into the lung interstitium. Venous return goes up, not down, when a person lies down, so the first choice describes the opposite change.
questions.explanation_pt: Deitar desloca sangue das pernas e do abdome para o tórax, então o **retorno venoso e a pré-carga aumentam**. Um ventrículo esquerdo insuficiente trabalha na parte plana da **curva de Frank-Starling** e não consegue ejetar o volume extra; as pressões do átrio esquerdo e dos **capilares pulmonares** sobem e o líquido passa para o interstício pulmonar. O retorno venoso aumenta, e não diminui, ao deitar, então a primeira alternativa descreve a mudança oposta.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman dies after many years of HFrEF with repeated episodes of pulmonary edema. At autopsy, both lungs are heavy, firm and rust-brown. Microscopy shows many alveolar macrophages filled with coarse golden-brown granules. The granules turn blue with the Prussian blue stain. Which pigment is in these macrophages, and where did it come from?
choices: Lipofuscin from lysosomal digestion of the cells' own membranes
Hemosiderin from red cells that leaked out of congested capillaries
Anthracotic carbon from inhaled polluted air
Bilirubin carried to the lung from hemoglobin breakdown in the liver
Melanin made by activated alveolar macrophages
questions.explanation: In chronic **left-sided heart failure**, high pulmonary capillary pressure lets red cells leak into the alveoli. Macrophages eat them and store the iron as **hemosiderin**, which the **Prussian blue** iron stain colors blue; these are the "heart failure cells" of brown induration. **Lipofuscin** is also a golden-brown "wear and tear" pigment, but it contains no iron, so it does not stain with Prussian blue.
questions.explanation_pt: Na **insuficiência cardíaca esquerda** crônica, a pressão capilar pulmonar alta faz hemácias extravasarem para os alvéolos. Os macrófagos as fagocitam e armazenam o ferro como **hemossiderina**, que a coloração de **azul da Prússia** (Perls) cora de azul; são as "células da insuficiência cardíaca" (siderófagos) da induração parda. A **lipofuscina** também é um pigmento castanho-dourado de "desgaste", mas não contém ferro e não cora com azul da Prússia.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman with 20 years of poorly controlled hypertension has 6 months of dyspnea on exertion. Blood pressure is 168/92 mm Hg, and pulse is 78/min and regular. With the bell at the apex and the patient lying on her left side, there is a low-pitched sound just before S1. ECG shows sinus rhythm and voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy. Echocardiography shows thick left ventricular walls, a small cavity and an ejection fraction of 64%. What produces the extra sound?
choices: Rapid passive filling of a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle
Sudden tensing of a prolapsed mitral leaflet
Turbulent flow across a narrowed aortic valve
Atrial contraction pushing blood into a stiff ventricle
Delayed closure of the pulmonic valve
questions.explanation: This is **HFpEF** from hypertensive **LVH**, and the sound just before S1 is an **S4**: in late diastole the atrium contracts against a stiff, poorly compliant ventricle. An **S3** is also linked to heart failure, but it occurs in early diastole and comes from rapid filling of a dilated ventricle, which does not fit a small, thick ventricle with a normal ejection fraction. Because an S4 needs atrial contraction, it disappears if she develops atrial fibrillation.
questions.explanation_pt: Trata-se de **ICFEp** por **HVE** hipertensiva, e o som logo antes de B1 é uma **B4**: no final da diástole, o átrio se contrai contra um ventrículo rígido e pouco complacente. A **B3** também se associa à insuficiência cardíaca, mas ocorre no início da diástole e vem do enchimento rápido de um ventrículo dilatado, o que não combina com um ventrículo pequeno, espesso e com fração de ejeção normal. Como a B4 depende da contração atrial, ela desaparece se a paciente evoluir com fibrilação atrial.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has type 2 diabetes and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. His HbA1c remains high on metformin, so a second oral drug is added. Over the next 6 weeks he gains 4 kg, his ankles swell, and he needs more pillows to sleep. He has had no episodes of hypoglycemia. Exam shows crackles at both lung bases and pitting edema to the mid-shins. Which drug was most likely added?
choices: Pioglitazone
Empagliflozin
Glipizide
Sitagliptin
Acarbose
questions.explanation: **Thiazolidinediones** such as pioglitazone activate **PPAR-gamma** and increase **sodium and water reabsorption** in the kidney. The result is weight gain, edema and possible **worsening heart failure**. Glipizide can also cause weight gain, through the anabolic effect of more insulin, but it usually causes hypoglycemia, not fluid overload with crackles; empagliflozin causes natriuresis and lowers heart failure hospitalizations.
questions.explanation_pt: As **tiazolidinedionas**, como a pioglitazona, ativam o **PPAR-gama** e aumentam a **reabsorção renal de sódio e água**. O resultado é ganho de peso, edema e possível **piora da insuficiência cardíaca**. A glipizida também pode causar ganho de peso, pelo efeito anabólico do aumento da insulina, mas costuma causar hipoglicemia, e não sobrecarga de volume com estertores; a empagliflozina causa natriurese e reduz as internações por insuficiência cardíaca.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 25% has new atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 132/min. He receives intravenous diltiazem for rate control. Thirty minutes later, his heart rate is 96/min, but his blood pressure has fallen from 118/74 mm Hg to 84/52 mm Hg. He is more short of breath, and there are crackles up to the middle of both lung fields. Which action of the drug best explains his worsening heart failure?
choices: Inhibition of the Na-K ATPase in myocytes
Blockade of fast sodium channels in ventricular myocytes
Less calcium entry through L-type channels into myocytes
Blockade of potassium channels that prolongs repolarization
Blockade of beta-1 receptors that lowers cAMP in myocytes
questions.explanation: Diltiazem is a **non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker**. It slows AV conduction, but it also reduces **L-type calcium entry** into ventricular myocytes, so less calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and contractility falls (**negative inotropy**). In HFrEF this lowers stroke volume and causes hypotension and pulmonary edema. Beta-blockers also depress contractility, but through beta-1 receptors and cAMP, and diltiazem does not act on these receptors.
questions.explanation_pt: O diltiazem é um **bloqueador dos canais de cálcio não di-hidropiridínico**. Ele retarda a condução AV, mas também reduz a **entrada de cálcio pelos canais tipo L** nos miócitos ventriculares, então menos cálcio é liberado do retículo sarcoplasmático e a contratilidade cai (**inotropismo negativo**). Na ICFEr, isso reduz o volume sistólico e causa hipotensão e edema pulmonar. Os betabloqueadores também deprimem a contratilidade, mas via receptores beta-1 e AMPc, e o diltiazem não atua nesses receptores.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman has long-standing severe tricuspid regurgitation and right-sided heart failure. She drinks no alcohol. Exam shows jugular venous distension with large v waves, a large pulsatile liver, ascites and leg edema. Aminotransferases and bilirubin are mildly elevated. A liver biopsy is done. Which histologic pattern is most likely?
choices: Periportal (zone 1) necrosis with fibrin deposits
Interface hepatitis with lymphoid aggregates in expanded portal tracts
Macrovesicular fat in zone 3 with Mallory-Denk bodies
Centrilobular (zone 3) sinusoidal congestion and hepatocyte loss
Noncaseating granulomas in the portal tracts
questions.explanation: High right atrial pressure is transmitted back through the hepatic veins to the **central veins**. **Zone 3** is closest to this outflow and farthest from the oxygen supply, so it shows **sinusoidal congestion** and hepatocyte loss; grossly this is the **nutmeg liver**, and long-standing cases can progress to liver fibrosis (cardiac cirrhosis). Alcohol-related injury also favors zone 3, but it shows fat and Mallory-Denk bodies, and she does not drink.
questions.explanation_pt: A pressão alta no átrio direito é transmitida pelas veias hepáticas até as **veias centrolobulares**. A **zona 3** é a mais próxima dessa drenagem e a mais distante do suprimento de oxigênio, por isso mostra **congestão sinusoidal** e perda de hepatócitos; macroscopicamente é o **fígado em noz-moscada** (*nutmeg liver*), e casos de longa duração podem evoluir para fibrose hepática (cirrose cardíaca). A lesão alcoólica também predomina na zona 3, mas mostra esteatose e corpúsculos de Mallory-Denk, e a paciente não bebe.
